title: Synchronizing evolving rep range with movement patterns, variations & rotations
summary: NH explains how to set evolving rep ranges across the variations of a movement pattern so they balance volume and intensity. Each lift gets its own range, an intense main lift is paired with a higher-rep variation, and lifts are organized as a tree by specificity. He treats upper and lower body trees as nearly independent for fatigue.
claims: The more advanced you are, the more flexible and complex the program must be; novices can stay simple and repetitive
About 90% of his lifts use evolving rep ranges
Each rep range represents a value of volume and intensity that must be clearly defined
A 2-20 evolving range is far too wide; it's a whole program's progression scheme, not one lift's range
8-12 leans toward volume, 15-20 more so; he never goes above 15 reps himself; 2-3 to 2-5 is intensity-based
Balance volume and intensity within a pattern: e.g. deadlift 1-3 or 2-4 reps paired with RDLs at 5-7, 5-8 or 5-10
Applying the same programming principle to an entire movement pattern eventually fails and stalls growth
Ideally the day you do the fewest deadlift reps matches the day you push RDL reps highest, e.g. 2 deadlift reps with multiple sets of 8 on RDLs
Evolving ranges are anti-sandbagging (6-10 should look like 10/9/8), but repeating slightly easy sets on the volume variation is fine to accumulate tonnage
When the intense range moves toward volume, the variation can push back to failure
For volume-preferring bench lifters: main bench at 6-10 and high-volume work at 12-15 or 15-18
He sees each movement pattern as a tree ranked by specificity: bench, spoto press, close-grip bench, push-up, diamond push-up, down to banded flies
Smart exercise selection does the work: RDLs and flies naturally suit higher reps; don't do flies for 3-5
A lift's rep tendency depends on its danger and its ability to resist muscular and structural failure
Give each lift its own rep range; small changes like 3x5 vs 5x5 or 6-10 vs 8-12 make a big difference in progression
Novices should apply evolving ranges only to strength work at first, keep variations static, then gradually spread evolving ranges
Teaching evolving ranges early makes them second nature; switching late is a culture shock, so go slowly
Lifts in the same tree (e.g. squat and deadlift) share fatigue; a brutal high-volume squat day means adapting the deadlift's range or variation
Communication between upper and lower trees is almost nonexistent; he hasn't seen CNS fatigue from deadlifts affect his bench
Overall recovery from food and sleep links both trees, and a smashed upper back can make you less tight on bench, but it's minimal
